meta.title: Hausa B1 Intermediate
meta.subtitle: 1000 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Hausa → English (see the Hausa, recall the meaning) and English → Hausa (see an English meaning, recall the Hausa). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 1000 words for an intermediate learner, aligned to B1 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand the main points of clear standard input on familiar matters regularly encountered in work, school, leisure, etc.' — a learner here is able to deal with most situations likely to arise while travelling, to produce simple connected text on topics that are familiar or of personal interest, and to describe experiences and events, dreams, hopes and ambitions and briefly give reasons and explanations for opinions and plans. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no exam board publishes a graded word list for Hausa, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — opinions and arguing a point, news, government and society, the law, money and the economy, work and business, education, health and the body, the environment, travel and its troubles, technology, the arts and media, religion and custom, character and relationships, and the verbs, linking words and abstract nouns connected speech is built out of — all 1000 words of it, since the levels below already teach every word that both English Wiktionary and the Tatoeba collection of Hausa sentences contain. Each word is counted in that collection by the WHOLE word (a noun's plural and its forms with the linker and the possessive endings added together). The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. Every headword is printed as Hausa is ordinarily written, in the Latin alphabet with its hooked letters (ɓ ɗ ƙ and 'y); beneath it, where English Wiktionary gives one, is the same word with its TONES and VOWEL LENGTH marked, which ordinary writing leaves out: a high tone is unmarked, a low tone takes a grave accent (à), a falling tone a circumflex (â), and a long vowel a macron (ā) — ruwā 'water', màcḕ 'woman'. 166 of the 1000 words have that line. 833 of the 1000 are glossed by Folio itself rather than taken from Wiktionary, which lacks some of the commonest words in the language (yi 'to do', tafi 'to go', da 'and, with'); those carry no tone line, since a tone that no source states is not printed. The nouns show their gender, masculine or feminine, and their plural, which in Hausa is seldom predictable, wherever the source gives them. Real example sentences come with 665 of the 1000 words, three apiece for 516 of them, with the word picked out in colour; the sentences are as Tatoeba's contributors wrote them, which is not always with the hooks. There is no read-aloud button: few devices carry a Hausa voice, and one without it reads the word in English. The Hausa Alphabet deck, the first in this collection, teaches the hooked letters and the other sounds English spelling has no letter for. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, tone, gender and plurals: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0), and Folio's own glosses for the words it lacks. Frequency and example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
